title: My King, I speak your praise
intro: Hakim Sanai of Ghazni (died about 1131), in today's Afghanistan, began as a court poet writing praise of the Ghaznavid sultans and ended as one of the first great Sufi poets. His *Hadiqat al-Haqiqa* ('The Garden of Truth') was the first long mystical poem in Persian, and Rumi wrote that he came 'following Sanai and Attar'. This short ghazal is a *monājāt*, a private prayer: it praises God as pure, beyond need, beyond description and beyond change, and ends with the poet's hope that a tongue that has spoken only of God's oneness will be spared the fire. Its simple words and dancing rhythm have made it a favourite of Iranian schoolbooks and singers.

lines.fa: ملکا ذکر تو گویم که تو پاکی و خدایی / نروم جز به همان ره که توام راه نمایی
lines.r: malekā zekr-e to guyam ke to pāki vo khodāyi / naravam joz be hamān rah ke to-am rāh namāyi
lines.en: My King, I speak your praise, for you are pure, you are God; / I will walk no road but the one you show me.
words: O King! – ملک 'king' + ـا of address
I say, I speak – no می
you are pure – پاک + ی 'you are'
you show me – the ـم 'me' is attached to تو

lines.fa: همه درگاه تو جویم همه از فضل تو پویم / همه توحید تو گویم که به توحید سزایی
lines.r: hame dargāh-e to juyam hame az fazl-e to puyam / hame towhid-e to guyam ke be towhid sezāyi
lines.en: I seek only your door, I run only by your grace, / I speak only of your oneness, for oneness is your due.
lines.note: Most printings add two couplets here, on God having no wife and no child; they are left out on this page.
words: declaring God one, the oneness of God

lines.fa: تو حکیمی تو عظیمی تو کریمی تو رحیمی / تو نماینده‌ی فضلی تو سزاوار ثنایی
lines.r: to hakimi to 'azimi to karimi to rahimi / to namāyande-ye fazli to sezāvār-e sanāyi
lines.en: You are wise, you are great, you are generous, you are merciful; / you are the one who shows grace, you are worthy of praise.
lines.note: The ـی at the end of each word is 'you are': حکیمی = حکیم هستی.

lines.fa: بری از رنج و گدازی بری از درد و نیازی / بری از بیم و امیدی بری از چون و چرایی
lines.r: bari az ranj o godāzi bari az dard o niyāzi / bari az bim o omidi bari az chun o cherāyi
lines.en: You are free of suffering and wasting, free of pain and need, / free of fear and hope, free of how and why.
lines.note: «بی‌چون و چرا» 'without how or why' is still everyday Persian for 'without question'.

lines.fa: بری از خوردن و خفتن بری از شرک و شبیهی / بری از صورت و رنگی بری از عیب و خطایی
lines.r: bari az khordan o khoftan bari az sherk o shabihi / bari az surat o rangi bari az 'eyb o khatāyi
lines.en: Free of eating and sleeping, free of partners and likenesses, / free of form and colour, free of fault and error.

lines.fa: نتوان وصف تو گفتن که تو در فهم نگنجی / نتوان شبه تو گفتن که تو در وهم نیایی
lines.r: natavān vasf-e to goftan ke to dar fahm nagonji / natavān shebh-e to goftan ke to dar vahm nayāyi
lines.en: No one can describe you, for you do not fit in the mind; / no one can name your like, for you do not come into the imagination.

lines.fa: نبد این خلق و تو بودی نبود خلق و تو باشی / نه بجنبی نه بگردی نه بکاهی نه فزایی
lines.r: nabod in khalgh o to budi nabovad khalgh o to bāshi / na bejonbi na begardi na bekāhi na fazāyi
lines.en: This creation was not, and you were; creation will not be, and you will be; / you do not move, you do not change, you neither shrink nor grow.
lines.note: Look at the two forms: نبد *nabod* 'was not', and نبود read *nabovad* 'will not be' – the same letters as نبود *nabud* 'was not', read in the old way.
words: will not be – the old present of بودن

lines.fa: همه عزی و جلالی همه علمی و یقینی / همه نوری و سروری همه جودی و جزایی
lines.r: hame 'ezzi vo jalāli hame 'elmi vo yaghini / hame nuri vo soruri hame judi vo jazāyi
lines.en: You are all glory and majesty, all knowledge and certainty, / all light and joy, all generosity and reward.
lines.note: Printings have one more couplet before the last; it is left out on this page.

lines.fa: لب و دندان سنایی همه توحید تو گوید / مگر از آتش دوزخ بودش روی رهایی
lines.r: lab o dandān-e sanāyi hame towhid-e to guyad / magar az ātash-e duzakh bovad-ash ru-ye rahāyi
lines.en: Sanai's lips and teeth speak only of your oneness, / in the hope that he may find a way of escape from the fire of hell.
words: lips and teeth – the whole mouth
in the hope that, perhaps (an old meaning)
he may have (lit. 'to him may be')

commentary:
**The ideas.** The poem is a list – and that is its power. Sanai piles up the qualities of God in short, balanced phrases: wise, great, generous, merciful; free of pain and need, of fear and hope, of eating and sleeping, of form and colour. It is a lesson in what theologians call the negative way: God is best described by what he is not, because nothing in our world is like him. He cannot be described or imagined, does not move or change; creation came after him and will pass before him. Only at the end does the poet appear, hoping that a mouth that has spoken of nothing but God's oneness will be saved.

**The rhythm.** The metre (*ramal*) breaks every half-line into four equal steps, *da-da-DUM-DUM* four times, and Sanai fills each step with a matching phrase: *ma-la-kā zek-re to gu-yam ke to pā-ki yo kho-dā-yi*. Most couplets also rhyme inside: [[جویم|juyam]] / [[پویم|puyam]] / [[گویم|guyam]], [[حکیمی|hakimi]] / [[عظیمی|'azimi]] / [[کریمی|karimi]] / [[رحیمی|rahimi]]. The end rhyme is the long [[ـایی|-āyi]]: [[خدایی|khodāyi]], [[نمایی|namāyi]], [[سزایی|sezāyi]], [[چرایی|cherāyi]]. It is a rhythm children can clap to, which is one reason they learn it.

**The grammar.** Almost every phrase ends in [[ی|-i]] 'you are': [[تو حکیمی|to hakimi]] 'you are wise', [[بری از رنجی|bari az ranji]] 'you are free of pain'. This is the short form of [[هستی|hasti]] that modern Persian still uses after a noun or adjective: [[تو خسته‌ای|to khaste-i]] 'you are tired'. The old verbs [[نبد|nabod]] 'was not', [[نتوان|natavān]] 'one cannot' and [[فزایی|fazāyi]] 'you increase' are easy to decode. The sixth couplet in modern prose: [[نمی‌شود تو را وصف کرد، چون در فهم نمی‌گنجی؛ نمی‌شود برایت شبیهی گفت، چون به خیال نمی‌آیی|nemi-shavad to rā vasf kard, chon dar fahm nemi-gonji; nemi-shavad barā-yat shabihi goft, chon be khiyāl nemi-āyi]].

**Using it.** [[ملکا ذکر تو گویم|malekā zekr-e to guyam]] is one of the classical poems Iranian children meet in their school Persian books, and it is often sung and recited at gatherings. Its vocabulary of praise is still alive, too: [[بی‌چون و چرا|bi chun o cherā]] 'without how or why' means 'without question', and [[ذکر|zekr]] is the word for the repeated prayers of Sufis.
